clue.text: The end of reason! Read with derision about 'cultural' politician

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of reason is used
about can mean scattered around, so the gathered letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a politician by reading aloud with scorn, declaring it the death of rational thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end of' gives N; 'about' rearranges the next two words. 'cultural' sits in quotes because she held the Culture brief, and the exclamation is the surface's own.
explanation.definitionFit: Nadine Dorries was the UK Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport when this was set, hence a politician tied to culture.

clue.text: Performances by non-female groups

indicators.note: non means not having, so the letter for female is removed from the word for groups

parts.note: factions are groups within a larger body

explanation.surface: A review of shows put on by all-male troupes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non' strips F from FACTIONS. 'non-female groups' reads as one phrase describing the performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Actions and performances are both deeds or acts carried out, so one stands for the other.

clue.text: Drive up motorway back to university

indicators.note: back means the preceding pieces are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written
MI (M1) is Britain's main north-south motorway
LSE is the London School of Economics, a university

explanation.surface: Directions for a trip up the motorway, then back to college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns UP plus MI into IMPU; 'to' joins on LSE. 'up' looks like a reversal signal but is the letters UP themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive here is a noun meaning an inner urge, the same sense as impulse.

clue.text: With space to move, Bale's dribbling worth utilising

parts.note: an em is a printer's unit of space
a ploy is a move or tactic

indicators.note: dribbling a ball moves it about, so the letters of the footballer's name are shifted around

explanation.surface: Given room to run, Gareth Bale dribbling the ball shows he is worth picking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dribbling' rearranges BALE into ABLE. Gareth Bale is a Welsh footballer, which makes 'dribbling' look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something employable can be put to use, so it is worth utilising.

clue.text: Alone? Head down for big city

indicators.note: the head letter is moved further down in this down entry

parts.note: solo means alone

explanation.surface: Someone lonely in a large city, head bowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head down' takes the S at the top of SOLO and drops it one place.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital of Norway, a major city.

clue.text: Charges still regularly included — is disconcerting

indicators.note: included means placed within, so the picked letters go inside the word for charges

parts.note: rates are charges, as in fees

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word still

explanation.surface: Fees still routinely included in a bill is unsettling news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the second and fourth letters of still; 'included' sets them in the word for charges. 'still' reads as 'yet', not as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle someone is to unsettle or fluster them, so rattles means is disconcerting.

clue.text: School in centre of Leek welcoming old money

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in, so the old coin goes between the picked letters
the centre of a word is its middle letters, here the two in the middle of Leek

parts.note: a ducat is an old gold coin

explanation.surface: A school in the middle of Leek takes in old money from a benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes Leek's middle pair; 'welcoming' wraps them round the coin. Leek is a Staffordshire town. 'School' is a verb here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or train them, which is what educate means.

clue.text: One managing to get politician to bite? Sadly fifty involved — shameful!

parts.note: Antonio Conte is a football manager, managing Tottenham Hotspur when this was set
MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: involved means taken in, so the Roman numeral goes inside the word bite
sadly here means in a sorry state, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone trying to make a politician take the bait, with fifty involved, sounds like a bribe and disgraceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' rearranges BITE to TIBE; 'involved' sets L inside it. 'One managing' looks generic but points to the football manager Conte.
explanation.definitionFit: Something contemptible deserves scorn, which is what shameful conduct earns.

clue.text: Most recorded and freely available

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its final letter

parts.note: something recorded is on tape

explanation.surface: The most recorded songs are the ones easily found anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most' trims the last letter from ON TAPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer on tap flows whenever wanted, so on tap means readily available.

clue.text: Top politicians not totally respectful at office, we hear

indicators.note: not totally means the final letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: polite means respectful

indicators.note: we hear means the word for office is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a bureau is an office

explanation.surface: Leading politicians who are less than courteous in the workplace, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not totally' cuts POLITE to POLIT; 'we hear' turns BUREAU into BURO by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The Politburo was the ruling committee of a Communist party, its most powerful leaders.

clue.text: Politician on peanuts wore rags — not you, anyhow!

indicators.note: to rag is to tease or mess about with, so the letters are scrambled
not means the letter for you is taken away from the scrambled letters

parts.note: U is textspeak for you, the casual spelling 'anyhow' hints at

explanation.surface: A badly paid politician dressed in tatters, though not you, at any rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rags' scrambles ON PEANUTS WORE and 'not' takes out U (you). Owen Paterson resigned in 2021 after a lobbying scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen Paterson was the Conservative MP for North Shropshire and a former cabinet minister.

clue.text: Overly catty sign during party — I'm not staying!

parts.note: too means overly

indicators.note: during means set within, so the star sign goes inside the word for party

parts.note: a do is a party
Leo, the lion, is the feline sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Someone making excessively spiteful gestures at a party announces they are leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' sets the star sign inside the party. 'catty' looks like spiteful but means cat-like: Leo the lion.
explanation.definitionFit: Toodle-oo is a jaunty British goodbye, the sort of thing said on leaving.

clue.text: Corruption returned — slippery types covering the whole range

indicators.note: covering means wrapped around, so the reversed word encloses the range letters
returned means the word for slippery types is read backwards

parts.note: eels are slippery creatures
A to Z covers the whole range

explanation.surface: Corrupt practice is back, with slippery people in on every part of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' makes SLEE; 'covering' puts AZ inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleaze is dishonest or immoral conduct, especially in politics, which is corruption.

clue.text: Punch egghead, real bastard (he's only little)

indicators.note: bastard as an adjective means impure or corrupted, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the head, or first letter, of egg is E

explanation.surface: A furious call to hit an intellectual who is a real swine, with a note that he is small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bastard' rearranges PUNCH, E and REAL. 'egghead' looks like a brainy person but gives just the first letter of egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A leprechaun is a small sprite of Irish folklore, so he is notably little.

clue.text: Bad vibe — shame what some politicians do

indicators.note: bad here means spoilt, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A gloomy remark about the poor atmosphere and disgrace surrounding politicians' conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges VIBE and SHAME.
explanation.definitionFit: To misbehave is to act improperly, which describes the conduct of some politicians.

clue.text: Run 12

definitions.meaning: in cricket a ... is a run scored when the ball passes the batter without being hit

explanation.walkthrough: '12' points to the answer at 12 across, used as a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bye is an extra run in cricket, and bye is also a shortened goodbye like toodle-oo.

clue.text: PM's returning for some bedroom activity

indicators.note: returning means the letters are read backwards

parts.note: Peel's: Sir Robert Peel was a British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister heading home to do something in the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' reads PEELS backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleep happens in the bedroom, so it is one bedroom activity, the innocent sort.

clue.text: God depicted by visual artist

indicators.note: depicted by means shown inside, so the letters sit across the two words

explanation.surface: A deity painted by an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depicted by' finds the letters spanning visuaL ARtist.
explanation.definitionFit: A lar was a Roman household deity, guarding the home.

clue.text: River bank home to beavers originally

indicators.note: home to means housing, so the picked letter is placed inside the word for bank

parts.note: a tier is a bank, a row set one above another

indicators.note: originally means taking the first letter of beavers

explanation.surface: A riverbank that first housed beavers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' gives B; 'home to' puts it inside TIER. 'bank' looks like a riverside but means a tier.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tiber is the river that runs through Rome.

clue.text: Previous promise to marry Elizabeth, US writer

definitions.note: the answer is a verb, an old-fashioned word for promising to marry

parts.note: Bet is a short form of Elizabeth
Philip Roth was an American novelist

explanation.surface: Someone once made a pledge to wed Elizabeth, an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Previous' marks the answer as old-fashioned usage rather than giving letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To betroth is an archaic verb for engaging, or pledging, someone in marriage.

clue.text: Stand in for Romeo priest found on top of woman

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece on top of another comes before it

parts.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Eli is the priest in the Bible who raised Samuel
Eve, the first woman

explanation.surface: A racy scene: Romeo stands in, and a priest is caught lying on a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found on top of' works because this is a down entry: the priest sits above the woman in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve someone is to take over their duty, which is to stand in for them.

clue.text: Politician clueless about way forward (with no drawback)? Possibly

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for clueless wraps the other letters

parts.note: lost means clueless, at a loss
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be arranged another way
with no means the following letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
draw read back gives WARD

explanation.surface: A politician with no idea of a way forward and keen to avoid any downside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes draw written backwards; 'Possibly' rearranges the remaining FOR into FRO; 'about' sets both pieces inside the word for clueless. The trailing 'Possibly' also teases the politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Frost was the UK's Brexit negotiator and a Cabinet Office minister in the Lords.

clue.text: Chippy might have this stew (used to be served up)

parts.note: to stew is to fret or worry

indicators.note: served up in a down entry means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: was means used to be

explanation.surface: A fish and chip shop menu: stew, once on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' turns WAS into SAW. 'Chippy' suggests a chip shop but is British slang for a carpenter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fretsaw is a fine-bladed saw, a tool a carpenter would own.

clue.text: Ofsted head right — 2's looking after school paperwork

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
looking after means holding in care, so the numeral wraps the word for school

parts.note: II is two in Roman numerals
a gam is a school of whales

explanation.surface: The head of the schools inspectorate is right: two people are caring for a school's paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looking after' wraps the numeral round the whales' school. Ofsted is England's school inspectorate; 'school' means whales, not pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the art of folding paper, so it is work done with paper.

clue.text: Disagree with British PM endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Clement Attlee was a British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Constantly arguing with a British Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' trims the final E from ATTLEE.
explanation.definitionFit: To battle with someone is to fight or clash, a strong way to disagree.

clue.text: Stranger's gang is back outside most of time

indicators.note: outside means wrapped round, so the reversed letters enclose the word for gang
back means the word is is read the other way round

parts.note: a crew is a gang

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A foreigner's gang has returned, out for most of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' makes SI; 'outside' wraps it round the gang; 'most of' drops the final A. 'Stranger' looks like a noun but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Screwy is slang for odd or crazy, so screwier means more odd.

clue.text: All you want's in Collins, they say

indicators.note: they say means the name is taken by how it sounds

parts.note: Phil Collins is a singer and drummer

explanation.surface: A claim that everything you could want is in a Collins dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collins' suggests the dictionary but means the musician Phil Collins.
explanation.definitionFit: To have your fill is to have as much as you want.

clue.text: Trio cease performing — they're largely unknown

indicators.note: performing suggests the letters put on an act and rearrange themselves

explanation.surface: A trio of musicians stops playing because nobody has heard of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'performing' rearranges TRIO and CEASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoterica are obscure items known only to a few, so largely unknown things.

clue.text: Political assistant old (and he's impotent)

parts.note: a spad is a special adviser to a UK government minister

explanation.surface: An elderly political aide, and a feeble one at that.
explanation.definitionFit: Spado is a legal and old term for a man who is impotent or castrated.

clue.text: Enter while rolling joint? This will ensure discipline in the house

definitions.text: This will ensure discipline in the house

indicators.note: rolling means tumbling about, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: the hip is a joint

explanation.surface: Someone comes in while making a cannabis cigarette, and the party bosses will want order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolling' rearranges ENTER and WHILE. 'joint' suggests cannabis but means the hip.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-line whip is the strictest party instruction to MPs to vote in the House of Commons.
